questions.stem: Which list contains only Earth hazards that originate mainly in the geosphere?
options: Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and sinkholes
Cyclones, droughts and lightning-induced fires
Floods, heatwaves and coastal storm surges
Tornadoes, hailstorms and severe dust storms
questions.explanation: Earthquakes, eruptions and sinkholes are driven by processes in the solid Earth, such as plate movement, magma and the dissolving of rock. Cyclones, droughts, heatwaves and storms begin in the atmosphere, even though they affect the other spheres.

questions.stem: Which Earth hazard is caused by sudden movement of rock along a fault?
options: A sinkhole
A lahar
A storm surge
An earthquake
questions.explanation: Stress builds up in rocks until they break or slip along a fault, releasing energy as seismic waves, which is an earthquake. A sinkhole forms when the ground collapses into a cavity, often in limestone, and a lahar is a volcanic mudflow.

questions.stem: A lahar swept down a valley below a snow-capped volcano soon after an eruption. What is a lahar?
options: A fast flow of water mixed with volcanic ash and rock debris
A fast flow of hot gas and ash that travels close to the ground
A slow flow of runny basaltic lava that spreads from a fissure
A cloud of carbon dioxide that collects in low-lying valleys
questions.explanation: A lahar is a volcanic mudflow, formed when ash and debris mix with water, such as meltwater from snow and ice on the volcano, or heavy rain. A fast, ground-hugging flow of hot gas and ash is a pyroclastic flow, a different hazard.

questions.stem: In 1986 a cloud of gas burst from Lake Nyos, a volcanic crater lake in Cameroon, and flowed down nearby valleys, killing more than 1,700 people. Why was the gas so deadly?
options: Carbon dioxide is denser than air, so it stayed near the ground and displaced the air
Sulfur dioxide reacted with water in the lake to form acid that burned the villagers
Hydrogen gas from the lake ignited when it reached the cooking fires in the villages
Steam from the lake was hot enough to scald people living in the valleys below
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from magma below had dissolved in the deep water of the lake. When it was suddenly released, the dense gas flowed downhill and pushed away the air, so people and animals suffocated. It was not a hot or burning gas.

questions.stem: Two earthquakes of similar magnitude strike cities of similar population. One country is wealthy and one is poor. Which outcome is most likely?
options: The same number of deaths in both, because the magnitude of the shaking is equal
Fewer deaths in the poorer country, because its buildings are smaller and lighter
More deaths in the poorer country, but higher dollar losses in the wealthier one
More deaths in the wealthier country, because it has more tall buildings to fall
questions.explanation: Poorer countries often have weaker building codes, less engineered housing and fewer emergency services, so more people die. Wealthier countries have more valuable buildings and infrastructure, so their losses in dollars are often larger even when fewer people die.

questions.stem: Why can an Earth hazard push families in a poor region deeper into poverty for years afterwards?
options: They lose homes, crops and income, and often have no insurance to rebuild
They gain new land from the disaster but are taxed heavily on its value
They must leave the region permanently because hazards always recur there
They are cut off from aid because international agencies help only cities
questions.explanation: When a hazard destroys homes, livestock, crops and workplaces, households without savings or insurance cannot recover quickly, and money spent rebuilding is not available for schooling or health. This cycle can keep people poorer than before.

questions.stem: After a large flood in a tropical town, health workers warn of an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease. What is the main cause of this risk?
options: Floodwater removes all the bacteria from the soil
Floodwater dilutes the salt in people's normal diet
Floodwater contaminates drinking water with sewage
Floodwater raises the air temperature in the town
questions.explanation: Floods overwhelm sewage systems and wash waste into wells and water supplies, spreading disease-causing microbes. Standing water also lets mosquitoes breed, which is a second health risk after floods.

questions.stem: Severe tropical cyclones Larry and Yasi crossed the north Queensland coast in 2006 and 2011. Beyond damage to buildings, which effect did they have on the region?
options: They increased banana production by bringing extra rain to the plantations for years
They had no effect on farming, because cyclones only damage coastal buildings
They spread banana plants south, so the crop is now grown mainly in Victoria
They destroyed most of the region's banana crops, cutting supply and raising prices
questions.explanation: Both cyclones flattened banana plantations around Innisfail and Tully, which grow most of Australia's bananas, so supply fell sharply and prices rose for months. This shows how a hazard affects people's livelihoods and the economy, not just buildings.

questions.stem: An earthquake on the sea floor generates a tsunami. Which description of the sphere interaction is correct?
options: An event in the geosphere affects the hydrosphere
An event in the atmosphere affects the geosphere
An event in the hydrosphere affects the geosphere
An event in the biosphere affects the hydrosphere
questions.explanation: The earthquake is a movement of rock, so it begins in the geosphere, and it displaces a large volume of seawater, which is part of the hydrosphere. The tsunami can then affect the biosphere when it floods coastal ecosystems and towns.

questions.stem: Lightning starts a large bushfire. Smoke spreads over a city, and heavy rain a month later washes ash into a river, killing fish. Which sequence of spheres does this show?
options: Atmosphere to biosphere, then atmosphere, then hydrosphere and biosphere
Geosphere to atmosphere, then biosphere, then hydrosphere and geosphere
Biosphere to hydrosphere, then geosphere, then atmosphere and biosphere
Hydrosphere to atmosphere, then biosphere, then geosphere and hydrosphere
questions.explanation: Lightning is an atmospheric event that ignites vegetation in the biosphere. The fire's smoke returns to the atmosphere, and later rain carries ash into the river, affecting the hydrosphere and the fish living in it.

questions.stem: A very large explosive eruption sends sulfur gases high into the stratosphere. What effect is this most likely to have on global weather over the following year or two?
options: No change, as the gases fall out of the air within a week
Heavy rain at the poles, as the ash melts the polar ice caps
Slight global cooling, as sulfate particles reflect sunlight
Strong global warming, as the sulfur traps outgoing heat
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide forms tiny sulfate droplets that stay in the stratosphere for months and reflect sunlight back to space, cooling the surface slightly. Ash falls out quickly, so it is the sulfate, not the ash, that affects global temperature.

questions.stem: On the Island of Hawaii, gases from the Kilauea volcano react in sunlight and moist air to form 'vog'. What is vog, and why is it a health concern?
options: A thick mist of steam that is too hot to breathe near the vent
A fine dust of volcanic glass that causes cuts to the skin
A layer of ozone that forms near the ground and blocks sunlight
A haze of sulfate particles and gases that irritates the lungs
questions.explanation: Vog (volcanic smog) forms when sulfur dioxide from the volcano reacts to form sulfate aerosols and acidic droplets. Breathing it can trigger asthma and other breathing problems. It is a haze of particles, not hot steam or glass shards.

questions.stem: Why do most large tsunamis start at subduction zones rather than at transform boundaries?
options: Thrust faults there move the sea floor up or down, lifting the water above
Transform boundaries occur only on land, so they can never displace any seawater
Subduction zones have the warmest ocean water, which expands suddenly
Earthquakes at transform boundaries are always deeper than at subduction
questions.explanation: A tsunami needs a large vertical displacement of water. Megathrust earthquakes at subduction zones lift or drop huge areas of sea floor, and the water above moves with it. Transform faults move rock mainly sideways, so they displace little water, even when they lie under the sea.

questions.stem: In the open ocean a tsunami may be less than a metre high, yet it can be many metres high at the coast. Why?
options: The wave merges with the tide, which adds several metres to its height at sea
The wave slows in shallow water, so its energy is squeezed into a taller wave
The wave speeds up in shallow water, so it piles up against the slower waves
The wave gains energy from the wind as it crosses the ocean towards the coast
questions.explanation: Tsunami speed depends on water depth, so the wave slows as the sea floor shallows near the coast. The back of the wave catches up with the front, and the same energy is packed into a shorter, much taller wave. A tsunami is not driven by wind.

questions.stem: In March 2011 a magnitude 9 earthquake off north-east Japan caused a tsunami that flooded the coast and the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. What does this show about Earth hazards?
options: One hazard can trigger others, so the total impact is greater
Earthquakes cause more damage than tsunamis in every case
Tsunamis only occur when an earthquake happens on dry land
Nuclear plants near the coast are never affected by hazards
questions.explanation: The earthquake triggered the tsunami, and the tsunami disabled the power plant's cooling systems, causing a nuclear accident. Most of the deaths were caused by the tsunami rather than the shaking, which shows how linked hazards multiply impacts.

questions.stem: In the February 2011 Christchurch earthquake, water-saturated sandy ground behaved like a liquid, and silt erupted onto streets. Which statement about this process is correct?
options: Liquefaction was caused by a tsunami flooding the city before the main shaking
Liquefaction made buildings sink and tilt, even where the shaking did not break them
Liquefaction happens only in solid bedrock, so it did not affect the buildings on sand
Liquefaction made the ground harder, so buildings on sand suffered less damage
questions.explanation: Shaking raises the water pressure between sand grains until they lose contact, so the ground loses strength and acts like a liquid. Buildings, roads and pipes then sink, tilt or crack. It affects loose, wet sediment, not solid bedrock, and it needs no tsunami.

questions.stem: Which type of eruption is typical of runny, low-silica basaltic magma, as at Kilauea in Hawaii?
options: Plinian, with ash columns tens of km high
Effusive, with lava flowing out gently
Explosive, with violent pyroclastic flows
Phreatic, with only steam and no magma
questions.explanation: Basaltic magma has low viscosity, so gas escapes easily and lava pours out in flows and fountains, building broad shield volcanoes. Plinian eruptions are the most explosive kind and come from viscous, gas-rich magma.

questions.stem: Why are volcanoes above subduction zones, such as Mount St Helens, usually far more explosive than hotspot volcanoes such as those of Hawaii?
options: Their magma comes straight from the core, so it carries much more heat to the surface
Their magma is richer in silica and gas, so it is viscous and traps gas until it bursts
Their magma is hotter and much more runny, so it flows quickly and blasts out of the vent
Their magma contains less water, so it cools quickly and blocks the vent entirely
questions.explanation: Subduction-zone magmas are andesitic to rhyolitic, with more silica and dissolved water. Silica makes magma thick and sticky, so gas cannot escape until pressure builds and the magma shatters explosively. Hotspot basalt is hotter and runnier, not cooler.

questions.stem: Which feature would most strongly indicate that a volcano produces explosive eruptions?
options: Thick layers of pumice and ash around a steep stratovolcano
Broad, gently sloping sheets of ropy basalt lava flows
Long, winding lava tubes running down the volcano's lower slopes
Lava lakes of runny basalt that fill the summit crater
questions.explanation: Pumice and ash form when gas-rich magma is blasted apart, and layers of ash and lava build steep stratovolcanoes. Ropy (pahoehoe) flows, lava tubes and lava lakes all show runny basalt erupting effusively.

questions.stem: The young volcanoes of south-east South Australia, such as Mount Gambier and Mount Schank, are maars and scoria cones. Why was water important in forming the maar craters?
options: Rain filled the crater after the eruption, which is what makes a cone into a maar
Rivers carved the crater out of soft ash long after the volcano had become extinct
Rising magma met groundwater, which flashed to steam and blasted out a crater
Seawater flooded the volcano and cooled the magma before it could reach the surface
questions.explanation: A maar forms when magma meets groundwater, as in the limestone aquifer of the region. The water turns explosively to steam, blasting a wide crater below ground level, often later filled by a lake. A lake filling a crater later does not make it a maar.

questions.stem: Which evidence in the thin clay layer at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary links the mass extinction to an asteroid impact?
options: A high level of oxygen, released when the asteroid burned in the air
A layer of coal, formed from forests flattened by the impact blast
A layer of rock salt, formed when the impact evaporated the oceans
A high level of iridium, rare in crustal rock but common in asteroids
questions.explanation: Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but more abundant in many asteroids, so a worldwide iridium-rich layer points to an impact. Shocked quartz and tiny glass spherules in the same layer, and the Chicxulub crater in Mexico, support this.

questions.stem: How could a large asteroid impact on land cause cooling across the whole Earth for months to years?
options: The crater would expose cold rock that chills the lower air
The blast would remove water vapour from the whole atmosphere
Dust and soot thrown into the atmosphere would block sunlight
The impact would push Earth into an orbit further from the Sun
questions.explanation: Ejected dust, sulfate aerosols and soot from fires would spread through the upper atmosphere and reduce the sunlight reaching the surface, an 'impact winter'. Photosynthesis would fall, collapsing food chains. An impact cannot move Earth's orbit noticeably.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how a large asteroid striking the ocean would affect several Earth systems?
options: It would produce a tsunami, shake the sea floor, send vapour and dust into the air and harm life
It would affect the hydrosphere only, because the ocean would absorb all of the impact energy
It would affect the atmosphere only, because the asteroid would burn up before reaching the sea
It would affect the biosphere only, because the impact would kill marine life near the site
questions.explanation: An ocean impact transfers energy to the water, producing a tsunami (hydrosphere), shakes and fractures the sea floor (geosphere), and throws water vapour and debris into the air (atmosphere). These changes then affect living things (biosphere).

questions.stem: In 1908 an object from space exploded in the air over Tunguska in Siberia, flattening trees over a huge area but leaving no crater. What does this show?
options: A body can cause great damage by exploding before it reaches the ground
Only bodies that hit the ground and form craters can damage Earth systems
The Tunguska object was too small to affect anything on the ground below
The trees were flattened later by a separate earthquake in the region
questions.explanation: The Tunguska object broke up and released its energy as an airburst several kilometres above the ground. The blast wave flattened forest over about 2,000 square kilometres, so an impact event does not need a crater to cause damage.

questions.stem: A thin layer of shattered volcanic rock fragments is found in shale of Ediacaran age in the Flinders Ranges, about 300 km from the Acraman impact structure in the Gawler Ranges. The fragments match the Gawler Range volcanic rocks. What is the best explanation?
options: They were carried by glaciers that moved slowly east from the Gawler Ranges
They are debris thrown out by the impact and deposited far from the crater
They were eroded from the Flinders Ranges and carried west by ancient rivers
They are ash from a volcano that erupted in the Flinders Ranges at that time
questions.explanation: The fragments match rocks at the impact site and occur in a single thin layer far away, as expected for ejecta thrown out by an impact. Volcanic ash would not be made of older, shattered Gawler Range rock, and rivers flowing from the Flinders could not bring Gawler rock there.

questions.stem: How can clearing forest from steep hillsides increase the frequency of landslides?
options: Clearing lowers the water table, so the slope is always saturated
Roots that bind the soil are lost, and more rain soaks in or runs off
Trees normally add weight that keeps the slope from moving downhill
Cleared soil dries out and becomes too hard to move during rain
questions.explanation: Tree roots hold soil together and trees take up water. Once they are removed, soil is weaker and becomes waterlogged in heavy rain, so slopes fail more often. Drier soil would be more stable, not less.

questions.stem: A city grows and replaces paddocks with roofs, roads and car parks. Why do flash floods in its creeks become more frequent?
options: More rain falls over cities because roofs attract storm clouds to them
More rain evaporates from hot roads, so the creeks fill from the air
Less water is taken from the creeks, so they are already full in storms
Less rain soaks into the ground, so more runs off quickly into the creeks
questions.explanation: Hard surfaces are impervious, so rainfall that once soaked into soil now runs off rapidly through drains into creeks, raising peak flows. This is why cities build detention basins and wetlands to slow run-off.

questions.stem: Injection of large volumes of wastewater deep underground has been followed by swarms of small earthquakes in some regions. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: The weight of the water at the surface presses the crust down and folds the rock
Fluid pressure in the rock reduces friction on existing faults, letting them slip
The water dissolves the rock completely, so the ground collapses into large caves
The water heats the rock to melting point, so magma rises and shakes the ground
questions.explanation: Raised pore-fluid pressure pushes the two sides of a stressed fault apart slightly, reducing the friction that holds it locked, so it can slip and cause an earthquake. The fault was already stressed; the fluid acts as a trigger rather than a heat source.

questions.stem: Pumping large amounts of groundwater from beneath a city on soft sediments can increase which hazard?
options: Tsunamis, as water drains from the coast
Cyclones, as moisture rises from the ground
Land subsidence, as the sediment compacts
Volcanic eruptions, as pressure is released
questions.explanation: Removing water from clays and silts lets their grains pack together, so the ground surface sinks. Subsidence can damage buildings and increase flooding. It does not trigger eruptions, tsunamis or cyclones.

questions.stem: Which building design helps a building survive strong earthquake shaking?
options: Base isolators that let the ground move beneath the structure
Heavy unreinforced brick walls that resist sideways movement
A large, heavy concrete roof that holds the walls down firmly
Rigid joints that stop every part of the frame from flexing
questions.explanation: Base isolators (rubber and steel bearings) let the ground shake while the building above moves much less. Heavy unreinforced brick and heavy roofs are especially dangerous, because they crack and fall during sideways shaking.

questions.stem: Before 2011 many towns on Japan's north-east coast had high tsunami sea walls, yet the 2011 tsunami overtopped many of them. Which evaluation is most valid?
options: Walls are useless against any tsunami, so building them was a complete waste of money and materials
Walls failed only because they were badly built, so taller walls alone will prevent all future deaths
Walls made the tsunami larger by reflecting it, so the towns would have been safer without them
Walls reduce risk for expected events, but warnings, evacuation routes and land-use planning are also needed
questions.explanation: Sea walls are designed for a chosen height of wave, and a larger event can overtop them. They still slow and reduce some waves, but people survive mainly by evacuating quickly, so warnings, drills, high ground and planning where to build are all part of reducing risk.

questions.stem: Cyclone Tracy destroyed most of Darwin's houses on Christmas Day 1974. Which response did most to reduce damage in later cyclones?
options: Seeding storm clouds each wet season to stop cyclones forming
Building sea walls around the city to block the cyclone's winds
Stricter building codes requiring houses to resist strong winds
Moving the city of Darwin inland, well away from the coastline
questions.explanation: After Tracy, building standards in cyclone regions were strengthened, with roofs tied down to walls and foundations, which greatly improved how houses performed in later cyclones. Darwin was rebuilt on the same site, and cloud seeding cannot stop cyclones.

questions.stem: Which set of measurements is most useful for warning that a volcano may erupt soon?
options: Swarms of small earthquakes, swelling of the ground and more sulfur dioxide
Falling air temperature, rising humidity and stronger winds at the summit
Lower river levels, more bushfires and fewer birds on the volcano slopes
Higher tides, warmer sea water and more seaweed along the nearby coast
questions.explanation: Rising magma cracks rock, causing small earthquakes, inflates the volcano, which GPS, tiltmeters and satellite radar can detect, and releases more volcanic gas. A combination of these signs is far more reliable than any one alone.

questions.stem: Australia's tsunami warning centre is run jointly by the Bureau of Meteorology and Geoscience Australia. Why are deep-ocean buoys with sea-floor pressure sensors used as well as seismometers?
options: They stop a tsunami from forming by absorbing the energy of the moving water
They predict an earthquake days ahead by detecting changes in ocean temperature
They confirm whether an earthquake has actually displaced water to form a tsunami
They measure the earthquake's magnitude more accurately than seismometers can
questions.explanation: Seismometers detect the earthquake within minutes, but not every large undersea earthquake makes a tsunami. Pressure sensors on the sea floor detect the change in the weight of water above as a tsunami passes, confirming it and showing its size, so warnings can be issued or cancelled.

questions.stem: A seismic hazard map gives a high probability of strong shaking at a site in the next 50 years, but scientists cannot say when an earthquake will happen there. Why can't earthquakes be predicted precisely?
options: Earthquakes give clear warning signs, but the data are too slow to transmit
The stress and friction on faults deep underground cannot be measured directly
Earthquakes occur at random places with no link to faults or plate boundaries
Seismometers cannot record earthquakes until they are larger than magnitude 7
questions.explanation: Faults release stress when it exceeds the friction holding them, but neither the stress nor the friction several kilometres down can be measured, and small changes decide the timing. Scientists can map where earthquakes are likely and how often, giving probabilities rather than dates.

questions.stem: Records show that a fault has produced large earthquakes at intervals of 180, 220, 150 and 250 years, and the last was 190 years ago. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: No large earthquake can happen for 60 years, until the longest interval is reached
The fault is no longer active, because the last interval has already been passed
A large earthquake is possible at any time, but the data cannot give its date
The next large earthquake will happen in exactly 10 years, at the mean interval
questions.explanation: The mean interval is 200 years, but the intervals range from 150 to 250 years, so the fault is already within the range in which past earthquakes occurred. Recurrence data give a probability over a time window, not a date. The variation also shows the risk could arrive sooner than the mean.

questions.stem: The moment magnitude scale and the Modified Mercalli scale both describe earthquakes. How do they differ?
options: Magnitude is a linear scale of shaking; Mercalli is a logarithmic scale of energy
Magnitude measures energy released; Mercalli intensity describes effects at a place
Magnitude describes damage at a place; Mercalli measures the energy at the focus
Magnitude is used only for deep earthquakes; Mercalli only for shallow earthquakes
questions.explanation: An earthquake has one magnitude, calculated from the energy released. Its Mercalli intensity varies from place to place, depending on distance, depth, ground type and buildings, and is based on what people felt and the damage seen.

questions.stem: On the moment magnitude scale, each increase of one whole number means about 32 times more energy released. About how many times more energy does a magnitude 8 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?
options: About 64 times
About 2 times
About 100 times
About 1000 times
questions.explanation: Two steps of about 32 times each give 32 x 32, about 1000 times the energy. Adding 32 + 32 to get 64 treats the scale as if it were linear, and 100 times confuses energy with the tenfold step in measured wave amplitude.
